title: Why Learning Rediscovers the Closed-Form Diagonal Regularizer
claim: Different learned regularizers adopt very different spectra yet all reach the same error as the closed-form baseline, showing performance saturation.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side: spectrum curves left, error-vs-window plot right, shared legend
description: Two line plots with a shared legend on the right. Panel (a), 'Learned spectrum', plots the ratio Γ_k/Γ_1 on a log y-axis against mode index k from 0 to 50. A dashed black curve shows the closed-form power law and rises steadily. The orange-yellow curve (M3) follows the dashed curve closely. The blue (M1) and red-orange (M2) curves rise more slowly and plateau well below it. Panel (b), 'Error vs T', plots median error P over rooms (log scale, 0.1 to 1.0) against the number of snapshots T (log scale). The dashed closed-form curve falls from about 0.75 to about 0.15. The colored circles for M1, M2 and M3 and the pink diamonds for LIR sit almost exactly on that curve. A dotted line shows the per-room oracle. The eye goes first to the overlapping markers on the dashed line.
caption: Learned diagonal regularizers learn different spectra yet reach the closed form's error. M3 follows the closed form, M1 and M2 learn flatter spectra that penalize high modes less (a, single runs). All three track the closed form's error, M2 slightly above at the longest window, and the mode-coupling LIR tracks it too (b). Lower $P$ is better, $1$ means no better than guessing zero. This is the saturation of [ref], which [ref] finds outside the diagonal family as well.
abstract: Recovering modal amplitudes from a few sensors requires regularization, and the shape of the penalty decides how strongly each mode is shrunk. The best shape depends on the truncation noise that discarded modes add to every measurement, which is unobserved and could be room-specific. We identify a diagonal saturation principle: for a single snapshot, isotropic truncation noise makes the Bayes-optimal Tikhonov shape a closed-form power law Gamma_k proportional to lambda_k^|s|, set by the prior alone and independent of the domain. The off-diagonal anisotropy equals the Herfindahl index H of the discarded-mode power exactly, Weyl's eigenvalue counting law fixes the number of discarded modes and hence H, and Berry's random-wave conjecture enters only through a diagonal term D, which we measure directly. Together they predict an approximately flat loss landscape over the penalty exponent, which leaves a learned diagonal regularizer little to gain from tuning the exponent per room. On simulated acoustic rooms the closed form stays within 5.83% of a per-room power-law oracle across observation windows, and three learned diagonal architectures track its error, the closest within a fraction of a point and none more than 3pp above it, while learning qualitatively different spectra. In the truncation regime no tested method consistently improves on the closed form, including Learned Iterative Ridge, which couples modes across layers. The framework extends to heat diffusion through a known Green's-function correction with no new free parameters.
